An **Action** is a named operation on an object. Declare it once and
it appears as:

- a **REST endpoint** at `/api/v1/actions/<object>/<action>`
- a **button** on the record detail page
- an **AI tool** (`action_<name>`) for Agents and the AI Builder — once
  you expose it to AI (`ai.exposed`, [below](#from-an-ai-agent))

You don't repeat yourself across three surfaces. One declaration; three
ways to call it. An action can also start a [flow](/docs/build/automation/flows)
(`type: 'flow'`) when the work takes more than one step.

## Declare an action

```ts
// src/actions/approve_invoice.action.ts
import { Action } from '@objectstack/spec/ui';

export const approveInvoice = Action.create({
  name: 'approve_invoice',          // lowercase snake_case (machine id)
  label: 'Approve Invoice',
  objectName: 'invoice',            // attaches to the invoice object
  icon: 'check',
  variant: 'primary',
  locations: ['record_header'],     // where the button shows
  description: 'Approve this invoice?',  // shown in the param dialog
  successMessage: 'Invoice approved',
  refreshAfter: true,

  // collect input before running
  params: [
    { name: 'note', label: 'Approval note', type: 'textarea' },
  ],

  // only show the button when the record is still pending
  visible: 'record.status == "pending"',

  // expose it to agents and the AI Builder as `action_approve_invoice`
  ai: {
    exposed: true,
    description: 'Approve a pending invoice, recording the approver and an optional note.',
  },

  // what it does — a sandboxed script body. `input` is the params bag;
  // `ctx.record` is a read-only snapshot, so the write goes through `ctx.api`,
  // which needs the `api.write` capability
  type: 'script',
  body: {
    language: 'js',
    capabilities: ['api.write'],
    source: `
      await ctx.api.object('invoice').update({
        id: ctx.recordId,
        status: 'approved',
        approved_by: ctx.user.id,
        approved_at: new Date().toISOString(),
        approval_note: input.note,
      });
    `,
  },
});
```

After `os dev` recompiles:

- `POST /api/v1/actions/invoice/approve_invoice` works
- The Invoice record page shows an **Approve Invoice** button
- The AI assistant can call `action_approve_invoice` — it is exposed to
  AI — if its skills allow

## Action types

The `type` field decides what the action does:

| `type` | What runs | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| `script` | A `body` — an L1 formula expression or sandboxed L2 JavaScript | Most cases — server-side logic, auditable, and AI-callable once exposed |
| `api` | An HTTP call to a `target` endpoint (`method`, `bodyExtra`) | Reusing data-API or platform endpoints |
| `flow` | Runs the flow named in `target` | Multi-step business processes |
| `url` | Navigates to the `target` URL | Deep links, redirect-style actions |
| `modal` | Opens the page/modal named in `target` | Custom dialogs |
| `form` | Opens the FormView named in `target` | Guided data entry |

```ts
// api type — reuse a data-API endpoint
Action.create({
  name: 'archive_order',
  objectName: 'order',
  label: 'Archive',
  locations: ['list_item'],
  type: 'api',
  method: 'PATCH',
  target: '/api/v1/data/order/{id}',
  bodyExtra: { archived: true },
});
```

Types other than `script` require a `target`. Whichever type, it is one
declaration — but `url`, `modal` and `form` actions run only in the UI, so
they never become AI tools.

## Calling an action

### REST

```bash
# the record id can go in the body, or in the path
curl -X POST https://app.example.com/api/v1/actions/invoice/approve_invoice/inv_123 \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"note": "LGTM"}'
```

Params are sent flat in the request body. The record id can be supplied
either as a trailing path segment (`.../approve_invoice/:recordId`) or in
the body. The response is your script body's return value (or the call
result for `api`-type actions).

### From the UI

Where a button shows is declared on the action itself: `locations`
(`record_header`, `record_more`, `list_item`, `list_toolbar`, …) and
`order`. The `visible` predicate then decides, record by record, whether it
renders. A list view can also name actions for each row and for a selection
of rows:

```ts
// One list view; the container and `data` are omitted (see Views).
{
  type: 'grid',
  columns: ['number', 'customer', 'amount', 'status'],
  rowActions: ['approve_invoice', 'reject_invoice'],
  bulkActions: ['send_to_customer'],
}
```

### With a flow

There is no flow node that calls an action. Go the other way: put the
multi-step logic in a flow, and start it from an action with `type: 'flow'`
and the flow's name in `target`:

```ts
// flow type — start a flow by name
Action.create({
  name: 'run_invoice_approval',
  objectName: 'invoice',
  label: 'Run approval',
  locations: ['record_more'],
  type: 'flow',
  target: 'approve_invoice',
});
```

### From an AI Agent

An action reaches agents only when its author exposes it to AI:
`ai: { exposed: true }` with an `ai.description` of at least 40
characters, as in the example above, on a type that runs without a UI
(`script`, `flow` or `api`). Exposed, it is the `action_<name>` tool in
ObjectOS's own agents and the AI Builder, and `run_action` for an
[MCP client](/docs/configure/mcp). Unexposed, it is invisible to agents
and refused if called.

If `approve_invoice` is exposed and in a skill the agent has, the LLM can
call it. Inputs come from the conversation; the same invoke-time checks
apply as if the user had pressed the button.

> *"Approve invoice INV-2042 with note 'verified by phone.'"*

## Permissions

Who may run an action is checked as the caller, when it is invoked —
the same way over REST, from a button, and from an agent:

1. **`requiredPermissions`** — capabilities the caller's
   [permission sets](/docs/configure/permissions/permission-sets) must
   hold. A caller missing one gets `403`.
2. **The subject record** — it is loaded as the caller. A record the
   caller cannot read is answered as not found.
3. **AI exposure** — an agent reaches only actions exposed to AI.
4. **UI gating** — the `visible` and `disabled` predicates (CEL,
   evaluated against `record`, `os.user`, and params) control whether the
   button renders or is greyed out.

What the action then does is trusted app code. A `script` body's reads
and writes run with the app's authority: record access and field-level
security do **not** bound them. A `flow` action follows the flow's
`runAs`. So declare `requiredPermissions` for anything sensitive, and
treat writing an action as a code-review-worthy act.

## Built-in actions

Every object gets these for free:

| Action | What it does |
|---|---|
| `create` | Insert a record |
| `update` | Update a record |
| `delete` | Delete (or soft-delete) a record |
| `restore` | Undo a soft-delete |
| `clone` | Deep-copy a record |
| `share` | Direct share with a user, team, position, business unit, or a unit and its subordinates |

Don't redeclare these — they follow the object's [lifecycle & capability flags](/docs/build/data).

## Auditing

Platform events land in `sys_audit_log`, an immutable trail with fields
including:

- `user_id` — the originating user
- `action` — the action name
- `object_name` and `record_id` — what was touched
- `old_value` / `new_value` — the change
- `ip_address` / `user_agent` — request origin
- `created_at` — when it happened

This is your first stop for *"who pushed the button?"* questions.

## Generating actions with the AI Builder

> *"Create an action `escalate_ticket` on `support_ticket` that sets
> priority to urgent and assigns it to the on-call engineer."*

The [AI Builder](/docs/build/ai-builder) generates the action metadata and
queues the change for approval. After approval, the action is callable from
REST, the UI, and — recursively — the AI itself.
